reason: The sources support 16 highly surprising, dual-sourced claims about the unique nested structure and mystery of Hoag's Object.
story: In 1950, astronomer Arthur Hoag spotted something bizarre in the Serpens constellation: a perfect, smoke-ring-like structure of hot blue stars surrounding a golden core of older stars. Initially, Hoag thought it was a planetary nebula or a gravitational lens tricking our eyes. But it was a real, extremely rare ring galaxy—now known as Hoag's Object—located 600 million light-years away and stretching slightly wider than our Milky Way. Classic ring galaxies are born from violent cosmic collisions, but there's no trace of any colliding galaxy nearby. The mind-bending twist? If you peer directly through the dark gap between Hoag's golden core and blue ring, at the one o’clock position, you will see another, much more distant ring galaxy. It is a one-in-a-million cosmic photobomb, nesting one impossible ring galaxy inside the gap of another.
angle: Peering through the dark gap of Hoag’s Object, a rare ring galaxy, reveals another even more distant ring galaxy perfectly aligned in the background.

claims.claim: Arthur Hoag discovered the ring galaxy Hoag's Object in 1950.
Hoag's Object is located in the constellation Serpens.
The galaxy lies approximately 600 million light-years away from Earth.
Hoag's Object spans about 100,000 to 120,000 light-years in diameter, making it slightly larger than the Milky Way.
The center of the galaxy consists of a dense nucleus of older yellow or reddish stars.
The outer ring of the galaxy consists of hot, young blue stars.
A dark, seemingly empty gap separates the nucleus from the outer ring.
A second, much more distant ring galaxy can be seen through the gap of Hoag's Object.
The background ring galaxy is located at approximately the one o'clock position in the gap.
Upon discovering the object, Arthur Hoag suggested it was a planetary nebula.
Hoag also suggested the object could be a peculiar or pathological galaxy.
Hoag hypothesized that the ring was an optical illusion caused by gravitational lensing.
The gravitational lensing theory was disproved by observations from more advanced telescopes.
Ring galaxies are extremely rare, representing less than 0.1% of all known galaxies.
Most classic ring galaxies are formed by a collision where a smaller galaxy passes through a larger disk galaxy.
There is no trace or evidence of a second colliding galaxy or collision fallout in Hoag's Object.

disputed: Whether Hoag's Object formed via bar instability: Noah Brosch proposed this theory, which Schweizer et al. disputed because the nucleus is spheroidal rather than disk-shaped, while Wakamatsu argued it remains a viable theory. A script should present this as an unresolved debate among astronomers.

The timeline of a potential collision or accretion: Some astronomers estimate that an encounter or accretion event occurred 2 to 3 billion years ago, while others note there is no physical evidence of collision fallout. A script should attribute the 2 to 3 billion years timeline as an estimate.
